title: Anytime-CBU: Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Consequence-Based Utility Scoring

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution aims to reduce the computational cost of Consequence-Based Utility (CBU) scoring by addressing the inefficiency of uniform rollout allocation, which wastes compute on candidates whose quality is clear after few rollouts. No prior paper explicitly addresses this specific inefficiency in CBU scoring. While papers like [6] and [10] discuss test-time compute scaling and adaptive allocation strategies, they do not target the specific inefficiency of uniform rollout allocation in CBU scoring. Thus, the purpose is **not covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism reformulates CBU scoring as a best-arm identification (BAI) problem and applies LUCB-style adaptive allocation with Beta-posterior confidence bounds, arm elimination, and early stopping. Papers [1], [4], [5], [7], and [22] all discuss LUCB-style adaptive allocation or related BAI techniques, including confidence bounds, arm elimination, and early stopping. For example, [5] generalizes LUCB for efficient best-arm identification, and [7] uses LUCB with successive elimination for overlapping multi-bandit problems. These primitives are substantively equivalent to the mechanism described here, even though the application domain differs. Thus, the mechanism is **covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses RealMath with two solver models (Qwen2.5-Math-7B and DeepSeek-R1-7B) against Uniform-CBU. Papers [6], [9], [10], and [19] evaluate test-time compute scaling or reasoning efficiency in LLMs using similar evaluation designs, such as comparing adaptive methods against uniform baselines or measuring reasoning accuracy improvements. For example, [9] introduces Certaindex to quantify answer stabilization during test-time reasoning, and [10] evaluates adaptive compute allocation strategies. These papers share the same evaluation design principles (adaptive vs. uniform comparison, reasoning accuracy metrics) despite differing benchmarks or models. Thus, the evaluation is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is LLM evaluation/test-time compute for mathematical reasoning. Papers [6], [9], [10], and [19] all operate in the same general application area of LLM evaluation and test-time compute scaling, including reasoning tasks. For instance, [6] studies inference-time compute scaling in LLMs, and [19] focuses on efficient sampling for reasoning tasks. While the specific sub-problem (mathematical reasoning) differs, the broader domain of LLM evaluation/test-time compute is shared. Thus, the domain is **covered**.
